source_refs.note: Chapter 27 exercise (PDF 175-177) solved: 10 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key printed), 12 short (b as four comparison tables), 6 construction response and 4 descriptive questions. Book corrections: MCQ V(c), Q2(b)(iii), Q3 heading, Q7.

blocks.prompt: I. Glucose is a building block for all, except:
blocks.explanation: Cellulose, glycogen and starch are all made of glucose units (27.1). Inulin is a polysaccharide made mainly of fructose units (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: II. Which one of the following is not an aldose?
blocks.explanation: An aldose has an aldehyde group (–CHO); a ketose has a ketone group (C=O). Glucose is an aldose whereas fructose is a ketose (27.1).

blocks.prompt: III. Which one of the following element is not present in all proteins?
blocks.explanation: Every amino acid contains C, H, O and N (–NH₂ and –COOH), so all proteins have them. Sulphur is present only in proteins that contain sulphur amino acids, e.g. where disulphide bridges form (27.2.1).

blocks.prompt: IV. In DNA, the linkages between different nitrogenous bases are:
blocks.explanation: The bases of the two chains are held by weak hydrogen bonds: two between A and T, three between G and C (27.5.1).

blocks.prompt: V. Which one of the following nitrogenous bases is not common to RNA and DNA?
blocks.explanation: DNA has A, G, C and T; RNA has A, G, C and U (27.5.1, 27.5.2). Uracil is found only in RNA, so it is not common to both.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (c) is printed 'thiamine', which is vitamin B₁, not a base; the base is thymine. Read as thymine, (c) would also be correct, because thymine is found only in DNA. Uracil (d) is the clear answer as printed.

blocks.prompt: VI. Waxes are the esters of:
blocks.explanation: Waxes are long fatty acid chains esterified to long-chain alcohols, e.g. beeswax (27.4.1).

blocks.prompt: VII. A cell membrane is made up of:
blocks.explanation: In water, phospholipids form a double-layered sheet (bilayer), polar heads outward and non-polar tails inside; it forms the structure of all cell membranes (27.4.2).

blocks.prompt: VIII. The bonds in protein structure that are not broken on denaturation.
blocks.explanation: Denaturation (heat, change of pH) breaks the weak interactions such as hydrogen bonds, so the chains open up, e.g. egg white hardens (27.2.1). The strong covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure stay.

blocks.prompt: IX. The backbone of nucleic acid structure is constructed by:
blocks.explanation: Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester linkages between the 3' and 5' carbons of the sugars, giving the alternating sugar-phosphate backbone (27.5).

blocks.prompt: X. Which element prevents the development of tooth decay:
blocks.explanation: Fluorine, taken as fluoride (a micro-mineral, 27 Minerals), strengthens tooth enamel and prevents tooth decay (beyond the chapter). Calcium and phosphorus build bones and teeth but do not specially prevent decay.

blocks.prompt: a) What role does glycogen play in the human body?
blocks.explanation: Glycogen (animal starch) is the storage form of glucose. Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles; when the body needs energy it is broken down to glucose, which keeps the energy supply and blood glucose (70-110 mg/dL) steady (27.1.1).

blocks.prompt:
b) Point out the main structural difference between the compounds in each of the following pairs.
i) Glucose and fructose
blocks.explanation: Both are hexoses with the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ (isomers).

rows: Fruit sugar, abundant in fruits and honey

blocks.prompt: ii) Cellulose and starch
blocks.explanation: Both are polymers of glucose, (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ; they differ in the type of glycosidic link and in branching.

rows: Glucose units joined by α-links (α-1,4; also α-1,6 in amylopectin)
Long unbranched chains (up to 2500 glucose units)
Chains held by strong hydrogen bonds: rigid, insoluble
Structural material of plant cell walls

blocks.prompt: iii) Competetive and non-competitive inhibition
blocks.explanation: Both inhibitors stop the substrate from binding at the active site (27.3.2).

rows: Inhibitor has the same shape as the substrate
Inhibitor is not like the substrate
Binds at the active site and competes with the substrate
Binds at another site and changes the shape of the active site

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Part iii) is printed 'Competetive'; the word is competitive.

blocks.prompt: iv) Glycolipids and lipoprotein
blocks.explanation: Both are compound lipids: lipids joined to another kind of group (27.4.2).

rows: Transport hydrophobic lipids (cholesterol, triglycerides) in blood

blocks.prompt:
c) Which class of biomolecule contains each of the following linkages? Describe the function of each linkage.
i) Glycosidic ii) Peptide iii) Ester iv) Phosphodiester
blocks.explanation:
i) Glycosidic (C–O–C): carbohydrates; joins monosaccharide units into di- and polysaccharides (sucrose, starch, cellulose).
ii) Peptide (–CO–NH–): proteins; joins amino acids into polypeptide chains, fixing the primary structure.
iii) Ester (–COO–): lipids; joins fatty acids to glycerol or a long-chain alcohol (fats, oils, waxes, phospholipids).
iv) Phosphodiester: nucleic acids; joins the 3' and 5' carbons of sugars through phosphate, giving a strong sugar-phosphate backbone.

blocks.prompt: d) How the tertiary structure of proteins is formed?
blocks.explanation: The polypeptide chain (with its α-helices and β-sheets) folds into a specific three-dimensional shape because of interactions between the side chains (R-groups): hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulphide bridges. This often gives a globular protein, e.g. an enzyme with its active site (27.2.1).

blocks.prompt: e) In what way fats and oils are different?
blocks.explanation: Both are triglycerides (esters of glycerol with three fatty acids); they differ in the kind of fatty acids (27.4.1).

rows: Made of saturated fatty acids (no C=C)
Contain unsaturated fatty acids (one or more C=C)
Mostly from plants, e.g. vegetable oil

blocks.prompt: f) Describe the structure of steroids. Write a note on the functions of cholesterol.
blocks.explanation:
Structure: steroids are not made from fatty acids but have lipid-like properties. They have a steroid nucleus of three cyclohexane rings (A, B, C) and one cyclopentane ring (D) fused together; many have an –OH group (sterols), e.g. cholesterol (27.4.3).
Cholesterol: a sterol that is part of cell membranes and is used to make bile salts, vitamin D and steroid hormones (beyond the chapter); it is carried in blood by lipoproteins (27.4.2).

blocks.prompt: g) Describe the mechanism of enzyme action.
blocks.explanation:
The substrate (S) fits into the active site of the enzyme (E), forming a temporary enzyme-substrate complex; the substrate is converted into products (P), which are released, and the enzyme is left unchanged, free to bind another substrate (27.3):
E + S → ES → E + P
This is explained by the lock and key model (Emil Fischer, 1894): enzyme = lock, substrate = key.

blocks.prompt: h) Why does an enzyme catalyze a reaction of only a specific substrate?
blocks.explanation: The active site of an enzyme has a unique shape that only one particular substrate fits, like a key into its lock (lock and key model). Other molecules do not fit, so they are not acted upon (27.3).

blocks.prompt: i) Name different RNAs and discuss their function.
blocks.explanation:
1. Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries the genetic blueprint copied from DNA in the nucleus to the ribosomes.
2. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): helps to make up the ribosome, where proteins are made.
3. Transfer RNA (tRNA): brings amino acids and translates the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of the protein (27.5.2).

blocks.prompt: j) What are some sources of potassium, iron, calcium, magnesium and zinc in our diet?
blocks.explanation:
Potassium: salt, meat, sea food, fruit juices, vegetables, lentils.
Iron: liver, meat, egg yolks, nuts, whole grains, beans, peas, lentils.
Calcium: milk and dairy products, greens, broccoli, salmon, sardines, beans.
Magnesium: green leafy vegetables, nuts and whole grains (beyond the chapter).
Zinc: meat, seafood, whole grains (Table 27.1).

blocks.prompt: k) What is the role of iron in the body?
blocks.explanation: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells and myoglobin in muscle cells; these carry oxygen (Table 27.1).

blocks.prompt: l) How enzyme inhibitors are important in our body and medicine?
blocks.explanation: Many drugs and antibiotics work as enzyme inhibitors: penicillin irreversibly blocks the bacterial enzyme transpeptidase, so the cell wall is not made and the bacteria die (27.3.2). Competitive inhibitors such as malonate show how a look-alike molecule can switch an enzyme off. In the body, inhibitors help control enzyme activity (beyond the chapter), but poisons act as irreversible inhibitors and can cause severe illness or death.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The section heading is printed 'Construction Response Questions'; it means Constructed Response Questions, as in the other chapters.

blocks.prompt: a. Why does the digestive enzyme pepsin have an optimum pH of 2?
blocks.explanation: Pepsin works in the stomach, where hydrochloric acid keeps the pH about 2 (beyond the chapter). Its active site has the right shape only at this pH; at a different pH the ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds of its tertiary structure change, the active site is disturbed and the enzyme is deactivated (27.3.1).

blocks.prompt: b. How condensation of sugars and condensation of amino acid are same?
blocks.explanation:
Both are condensation reactions: two units join by a covalent bond and a molecule of water is eliminated, and repeating it gives a polymer.
Sugars: –OH + HO– → glycosidic link C–O–C + H₂O (glucose + fructose → sucrose; many glucose → starch, cellulose) (27.1)
Amino acids: –COOH + H₂N– → peptide link –CO–NH– + H₂O (polypeptides, proteins) (27.2.1)
Both are reversed by hydrolysis.

blocks.prompt: c. Why is cholesterol included in the lipid family?
blocks.explanation: Lipids are grouped by their properties: they are hydrophobic, insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. Cholesterol, a steroid, is not made from fatty acids, but it has these lipid-like properties, so it is a derived lipid (27.4, 27.4.3).

blocks.prompt: d. Why fats and oils are also called triacylglycerols?
blocks.explanation: Each molecule is an ester of one glycerol molecule with three fatty acids: all three –OH groups of glycerol carry an acyl group (R–CO–). Three (tri) acyl groups on glycerol give the name triacylglycerol (triglyceride) (27.4.1).

blocks.prompt: e. How hydrogen bonding is important in the double helix of DNA?
blocks.explanation: Hydrogen bonds hold the two chains of the double helix together through base pairs: A pairs with T by two hydrogen bonds and G with C by three (27.5.1). Each bond is weak, so the chains can separate for replication and transcription, but together the many bonds keep the helix stable. Because only A–T and G–C fit, the base sequence is copied accurately.

blocks.prompt: f. If the sequence T-A-C-C-G-A located on one strand of DNA, what sequence would be seen opposite to it on the other strand?
blocks.explanation:
A always pairs with T and G with C (27.5.1):
Given strand: T-A-C-C-G-A
Opposite strand: A-T-G-G-C-T

blocks.prompt: Q4. Classify and describe the structure of polysaccharides.
blocks.explanation:
Polysaccharides are large molecules of many monosaccharide units joined by glycosidic links, general formula (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ; on hydrolysis they give monosaccharides. Examples: starch, glycogen, cellulose and pectin (27.1).
Classification by function:
A. Storage polysaccharides
1. Starch: the main energy store of plants (potato, rice, grains), made of glucose units. It has two parts:
• Amylose: long unbranched chains of glucose joined by α-1,4 glycosidic links; insoluble in water.
• Amylopectin: compact, highly branched; α-1,4 links in the chains and α-1,6 links at the branch points; soluble in water.
2. Glycogen (animal starch): polymer of glucose stored in the liver and muscles; its structure is like amylopectin but even more highly branched.
B. Structural polysaccharides
3. Cellulose: the main structural material of plant cell walls; long unbranched chains of up to 2500 glucose units joined by β-links. The chains form strong hydrogen bonds with each other, so cellulose is rigid and insoluble in water. In food it is fibre, which improves gut health.
Classification by shape: unbranched (amylose, cellulose) and branched (amylopectin, glycogen).

blocks.prompt: Q5. How the structure of proteins support its function. Describe at each structure level.
blocks.explanation:
A protein's function depends on its exact three-dimensional shape, which is built up in four levels (27.2.1):
1. Primary structure: the specific linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. It decides how the chain folds and so its function; e.g. albumin (about 400 amino acids) and insulin need their exact sequence. A change of one amino acid can impair function, e.g. abnormal haemoglobin in sickle cell anaemia.
2. Secondary structure: hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups give regular patterns: the α-helix (bonds along one chain, coiled, e.g. keratin) and the β-pleated sheet (bonds between neighbouring strands, e.g. silk fibroin). These give stability and flexibility.
3. Tertiary structure: the chain folds into a 3D shape through interactions of the R-groups: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulphide bridges. In enzymes this makes the precise active site that binds the substrate; any change affects activity.
4. Quaternary structure: two or more folded chains (subunits) associate by the same interactions.
Shape and function: fibrous proteins (long, parallel chains linked by hydrogen or disulphide bonds; insoluble, strong) are structural, e.g. collagen, keratin, myosin; globular proteins (spherical) are working proteins such as enzymes and hormones. Keratin is not easily denatured because of its disulphide bonds.
When heat or pH breaks these bonds (denaturation), the shape is lost and so is the function, e.g. egg white hardens on heating and casein coagulates with lemon juice.

blocks.prompt: Q6. Write an account of classification of lipids with suitable examples.
blocks.explanation:
Lipids are hydrophobic compounds, soluble in organic solvents; they are not polymers. They are classified by chemical composition (27.4):
1. Simple lipids: esters of fatty acids with alcohols.
• Fats and oils (triglycerides): one glycerol + three fatty acids. Fats (saturated fatty acids) are solid, e.g. ghee; oils (unsaturated) are liquid, e.g. vegetable oil. They store energy and insulate.
• Waxes: long fatty acid chains esterified to long-chain alcohols; water-repelling coatings, e.g. beeswax, plant waxes.
2. Compound (complex) lipids: esters of fatty acids with alcohols carrying an extra group.
• Phospholipids: glycerol + two fatty acids + a phosphate group; polar head and non-polar tails; form the bilayer of cell membranes.
• Glycolipids: lipids with carbohydrate groups, mostly in nervous tissue.
• Lipoproteins: lipid-protein complexes that transport cholesterol and triglycerides in blood.
3. Derived lipids: hydrolytic products of simple and compound lipids with lipid properties, e.g. fatty acids, glycerol, steroids and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
• Steroids: four fused rings (A, B, C six-membered; D five-membered), e.g. cholesterol, bile salts, vitamin D, steroid hormones.
• Terpenes: plant hydrocarbons built from isoprene units, e.g. limonene; those with 40 carbons are carotenoids (27.4.3).

blocks.prompt: Q7. What are nucleic acids? Describe the roll of DNA and RNA in the protein synthesis.
blocks.explanation:
Nucleic acids are large biomolecules that store and transmit genetic information. They are polymers of nucleotides (sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base) joined by phosphodiester links between the 3' and 5' carbons of the sugars; the sugar is deoxyribose in DNA and ribose in RNA (27.5).
Role of DNA: DNA in the nucleus is the coded plan (blueprint) for proteins; each gene, a section of DNA, carries the instructions for one protein, coded in the sequence of the four bases (a codon of three bases codes for one amino acid). DNA replicates so that each new cell gets the full instructions (27.5.1).
Role of RNA and the steps of protein synthesis (27.5.3):
1. Transcription: the instructions of a DNA gene are copied into mRNA (by RNA polymerase) in the nucleus.
2. The complete mRNA leaves the DNA, goes into the cytoplasm and attaches to ribosomes (made with rRNA).
3. Translation: at the ribosome the code of mRNA is read; tRNA brings the matching amino acids, which are arranged in the order of the bases of mRNA.
4. The amino acids join by peptide bonds; the polypeptide chain grows until the complete protein is formed.
Flow of information: DNA → (transcription) mRNA → (translation) protein.
